technical.lead: Moonshot ships Kimi K3 weights under a revenue-gated licence
technical.body: Moonshot AI published the Kimi K3 weights on Hugging Face on Monday, July 27, and the constraint that matters sits in the paperwork rather than the architecture. The model card describes a 2.8-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts with 104 billion parameters active per token, 16 of 896 experts selected per token, and 93 layers split between 69 Kimi Delta Attention blocks and 24 gated-MLA blocks, with a 1,048,576-token context window and native vision through a 401-million-parameter MoonViT-V2 encoder; the weights ship as MXFP4 with MXFP8 activations produced by quantization-aware training rather than by rounding afterwards. At maximum reasoning effort the card's own evaluation table lists 93.5 on GPQA Diamond, 88.3 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 67.5 on DeepSWE. What the repository does not carry is Apache 2.0 or MIT. It carries a bespoke Kimi K3 License, tagged on Hugging Face simply as other, whose grant is otherwise MIT-shaped — run, deploy, fine-tune, modify, distribute, sell — with two commercial gates added. Any Model-as-a-Service operator whose revenue together with its affiliates passes 20 million US dollars across any consecutive twelve months must sign a separate agreement with Moonshot before using the model at all; any commercial product above 100 million monthly active users or 20 million dollars of monthly revenue must display the Kimi K3 name prominently in its user interface. Internal use, and access bought through Moonshot's own products or its certified inference partners, are carved out of both gates. Moonshot's own framing is open weight, not open source. The physical artifact is 1.56 TB across 96 safetensors shards, and vLLM — which shipped serving support the same day, with a Kimi Delta Attention prefix-caching implementation contributed by the Kimi team — puts the hardware floor at a single 8-way B300 node, with 16 B200s also supported, and measures 111 tokens per second per user at TP8 and 118 at TP16 on GB300 NVL72 at batch size one, rising to 331 and 370 respectively with its DSpark speculative decoder, roughly a threefold gain. AMD's MI355X is supported at launch alongside Hopper and Blackwell. For anyone without a rack, OpenRouter lists the hosted model at 3 dollars per million input tokens and 15 dollars per million output.

technical.lead: Thirty-seven firms join NVIDIA's Open Secure AI Alliance
technical.body: NVIDIA turned this month's Hugging Face intrusion into the founding argument for a new industry body, announced on Monday, July 27. The Open Secure AI Alliance launches with thirty-seven named inaugural partners, among them Microsoft, IBM, Red Hat, Cisco, Cloudflare, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks, Dell Technologies, HPE, Databricks, Snowflake, Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow, Siemens, Palantir, Capital One, DoorDash, NAVER, SK Telecom, Synopsys, Cadence, Elastic, LangChain, Cognition, Reflection AI, Nous Research, Thinking Machines Lab, OpenClaw, the Linux Foundation, and Hugging Face itself as the party that was breached. The declared scope is the whole agent stack — identity, permissions, isolation, guardrails, logs, model formats, multi-model scanning and secure coding workflows — built on top of work already running in the Linux Foundation's Akrites initiative and the OpenSSF community. Six projects went on the table at formation. NVIDIA contributed the NVIDIA Labs Object-Oriented Agent (NOOA), an open-source research framework now on GitHub that lets an agent harness integrate with a model so behaviour is easier to test, trace, audit and govern; Hugging Face contributed Safetensors; HPE contributed SPIFFE and SPIRE; IBM and Red Hat contributed Lightwell for signed patch distribution; Microsoft contributed MDASH, a multi-model agentic scanning harness; and SpaceXAI open-sourced Grok Build, a terminal-based AI coding agent, alongside a stated plan to open source the weights of the Grok line of models. NVIDIA's stated rationale is operational rather than ideological. During the Hugging Face incident, closed models could not distinguish an attacker from a defender and blocked the forensic work, so Hugging Face ran the open-weight GLM 5.2 on its own infrastructure to reconstruct more than 17,000 recorded actions and contain the intrusion. NVIDIA's position is that misuse risk is real for open models but is not unique to them, and that defenders lose most when they cannot inspect, adapt and run advanced models on their own hardware. The roster is as informative for its gaps as for its names: OpenAI, Google and Anthropic are not on it.

technical.lead: NVIDIA weighs a $250B backstop for OpenAI's Ohio campus lease
technical.body: The Wall Street Journal reported on Monday, July 27 that NVIDIA is in talks to guarantee roughly 250 billion dollars of the financing behind OpenAI's lease of a ten-gigawatt data-centre campus at Piketon, Ohio, on the former Portsmouth Gaseous Diffusion Plant site, developed by SoftBank-backed SB Energy, with a separate negotiation covering as much as 350 billion dollars to finance the NVIDIA chips that would fill it. The first phase is 800 megawatts targeting 2028. The reason a chip vendor is being asked to stand behind its own customer's rent is specific and unflattering: OpenAI does not hold an investment-grade credit rating, so what lenders would be lending against is NVIDIA's balance sheet rather than OpenAI's. Reuters could not independently confirm the report, terms are unsettled, and pricing, duration, collateral and repayment are all undisclosed; neither company commented. For scale against NVIDIA's existing book, its disclosed guarantee exposure is reported at 3.5 billion dollars with 712 million in escrow, and it closed its January fiscal year with 62.6 billion dollars in cash. The report lands three days after NVIDIA and SK Group signed a letter of intent on Friday, July 24 for a partnership valued above 500 billion dollars, covering a two-gigawatt SK Telecom AI factory and long-term AI-memory supply from SK hynix — the first factory built on NVIDIA's DSX platform, with Vera Rubin accelerators and HBM4, targeted for 2027. The market's verdict arrived in the same session: NVIDIA closed roughly 5% lower, AMD about 5% and Teradyne about 4%, the VanEck Semiconductor ETF lost more than 2%, and Sandisk fell about 11% on memory weakness following a large Shanghai listing by a Chinese memory manufacturer. A slide of more than 8% in crude lifted the Dow 0.51%, while the Nasdaq closed 0.18% lower and the S&P 500 was flat.

technical.lead: Unsloth routes ROCm-orphaned AMD cards to a Vulkan llama.cpp build
technical.body: Unsloth's hardware coverage grew sideways rather than upward on Monday, July 27. A change merged into main at 13:57 UTC teaches the installer to reach for a Vulkan llama.cpp backend instead of a HIP one. Until now the installer shipped HIP prebuilts exclusively, so older AMD parts sitting below the HIP minimum — the change names the RX 480 — received an install that could not actually run. Three things move. Users can opt in explicitly through UNSLOTH_LLAMA_BACKEND=vulkan, UNSLOTH_FORCE_VULKAN=1 or a --llama-backend vulkan flag, and that preference now persists in configuration across updates. On Windows AMD hosts whose GPU architecture is identifiable but absent from the HIP prebuilt, the installer switches to Vulkan on its own rather than shipping a dead build. And a machine holding both a supported and an unsupported card still defaults to HIP unless told otherwise. The routing respects ROCm family labels and special-cases gfx1103, the Phoenix and 780M part, with twenty routing tests behind it. A second change landed the same day on the offline path: tokenizer loads made with local_files_only no longer reach the Hub for metadata on transformers 4.57.2 through 5.5.4, resolving the cached snapshot locally instead, with matching treatment in the vision processor and the save paths. Neither change is installable yet. The newest tag is still v0.1.501-beta, the AMD-support release cut on July 20, so both currently exist only on the main branch.

technical.lead: Hot Chips early rate ends Friday, July 31, four days out
technical.body: The nearest hard deadline on this calendar is still a registration cutoff rather than a keynote, and it is four days out: Hot Chips 2026 stops issuing the early rate at 11:59 PM PDT on Friday, July 31, and accepts refund requests through 11:59 PM PDT on Wednesday, August 19, ahead of the symposium itself on August 23-25 at Stanford's Memorial Auditorium, which opens with a Sunday tutorial day running memory-technology and RISC-V tracks. The second real deadline is eleven days out: SecurityWeek's AI Risk Summit at the Ritz-Carlton in Half Moon Bay, August 11-12, steps its full-conference rate from $1,895 to $2,195 after Friday, August 7. Between those two dates sits the nearest Bay Area silicon event, FMS: The Future of Memory and Storage, August 4-6 at the Santa Clara Convention Center, whose Thursday main-stage executive AI panel is hosted by NVIDIA alongside KIOXIA, Samsung, Supermicro and VAST; the AI Infra Summit takes the same hall September 15-17, with keynotes from Google's Jeff Dean, Intel's Lip-Bu Tan and NVIDIA's Ian Buck across five technical tracks. The AI-security track clusters in early August: Black Hat USA runs August 1-6 at Mandalay Bay in Las Vegas with its AI Summit on Tuesday, August 4, and DEF CON 34 follows August 6-9 at the Las Vegas Convention Center West Hall, its AI Village running capture-the-flag against agentic systems; DEF CON says the postponement of its Middle East edition in Bahrain over regional security concerns leaves the Las Vegas dates unaffected. New on the developer and infrastructure track: AGNTCon and MCPCon North America, the Agentic AI Foundation's flagship under the Linux Foundation, runs October 22-23 in San Jose around the Model Context Protocol, the Goose agent framework and the AGENTS.md specification, its call for proposals having closed June 7; Newcomer's Machine Earning AI Summit lands September 29 in San Francisco, the same calendar day as OpenAI DevDay at Fort Mason and the opening of The AI Conference at Pier 48; and the invite-only Cerebral Valley AI Summit returns to San Francisco on November 12. On AI Tinkerers the position has not improved: the global calendar lists nothing in San Francisco or Palo Alto through the start of August, with Valencia, Manizales, Calgary and Seattle on the 28th, six more cities on the 29th, eight on the 30th, New York on August 1 and London on August 2. So the Palo Alto chapter's meetup on Tuesday, August 18, 6:30 to 9 PM PDT — apply-to-attend, roughly 150 places, Dyssonance AI sponsoring — remains the nearest Bay Area date carried here, and the San Francisco chapter's August 9 listing that keeps surfacing in search should still be treated as closed rather than upcoming: it resolves to an old page, and August 9 falls on a Sunday this year. The rest of the track is unchanged. Ai4 at The Venetian in Las Vegas August 4-6; Ray Summit at the San Francisco Marriott Marquis August 24-26, co-locating the vLLM Conference on the same pass with an agenda naming Robert Nishihara, Ion Stoica and NVIDIA's Bryan Catanzaro; the ACM AI Leadership Summit in Atlanta August 30 through September 2; OpenAI DevDay at Fort Mason September 29, applications already closed; The AI Conference at Pier 48 September 29 through October 1, whose September 29 opening track has sold out; the Runway AI Summit September 30; World Summit AI in Amsterdam October 7-8; the OCP Global Summit October 12-15 in San Jose; the AI Security Summit's San Francisco flagship October 15, two tracks across 45-plus sessions and 75-plus speakers with talk submissions still open; PyTorch Conference in San Jose October 20-21; NVIDIA's GTC Berlin October 20-22; GitHub Universe at Fort Mason October 28-29; SANS's AI Cybersecurity Summit in Arlington November 2-3, hybrid, hotel block closing October 9; OWASP Global AppSec USA at the Hyatt Regency San Francisco November 5-6, training from November 2; the application-only AI Engineer Code Summit in San Francisco November 11-13, speaker submissions closing October 11; the 19th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security in The Hague November 15, co-located with the 33rd ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security, its paper deadline closed firm on July 24 with notifications September 3 and camera-ready September 16; SC26 in Chicago November 15-20; AWS re:Invent November 30 through December 4; NeurIPS in December; IEEE-RAS Humanoids in Santa Clara December 6-9, whose call for papers closed July 24 with 200-plus submissions expected; and The AI Summit New York December 9-10. NVIDIA's GTC does not return to San Jose until March 2027.
